transcript: Here's all the theater I saw in March and what I thought of it. Heads up, I'm skipping over these four shows because I already made individual videos about them. First up, the life and slimes of Marc Summers. He was the host of Nickelodeon's Double Dare, and he's telling his life story. Show incorporates interactive game show elements that tie into his experience with OCD, which is a major focus of the show. I actually wish they'd leaned into that concept further, because the standard autobiographical stuff around the game show concept was not as interesting to me. But I did get selected as an audience volunteer to play Double Dare, and I won. Next up, stalker. This is a magic show from Swedish illusionist Brynoff and young. I personally like magic shows. This one was nicely structured around its central theme, and, yeah, it was good. The effect is a revival of a pretty recent play by Lucy Preble. I saw a different production of it in 2016, and I didn't love it, but I liked it. I had some of the same issues with the script this time around, but I do think it's a good play, and I really liked Jamie Lloyd's direction of this revival. Dead Outlaws, a new musical by the team behind The Band's Visit, telling the true story of an inept outlaw whose corpse ends up getting used as a sideshow attraction. So it's a fascinating story about exploitation and theft. I Loved the score in the direction. I will say the second half lost a little bit of steam for me, but overall I really enjoyed this. Sally and Tom is a new play by Susan Laurie Parks about a theater company putting on a play about Sally Hemmings and Thomas Jefferson. I kind of struggled with this one. I think it might have gone over my head a little bit. Like, I could see the parallels that she was drawing, but the specific way that they all came together, it didn't really click for me. But I would be curious to hear or read other people's analysis of it, because I could definitely be. Symphony of rats is the new production by Wooster Group, one of the more prominent experimental companies in New York. This is a reimagined revival of Richard Foreman's play about a president of the United States who believes he's getting telepathic messages from outer space. The show is extremely weird, sometimes in an amusing way, sometimes kind of exhausting. But it's Wooster Group doing their thing as usual. I was lucky enough to attend the invited dress rehearsal of cabaret, which I already have two videos talking about this production from when I saw it in London. I'll tag those below. I mostly stand by everything I said, which was mostly positive. I really like this production overall, but I'm really glad I got to see this cast. Bebe Neuwirth is phenomenal. Onto blanks and wood is Fantastic as always. I'm especially glad that I saw Eddie Redmayne because his performance is so specifically crafted with what this production is doing. Conceptually, the take on the character landed a lot better for me with the choices that he made in the role specifically. And that's it for March.
